geo.title: What to know
geo.body:
This assessment covers G.QP.1, G.QP.2, G.QP.3, G.T.1d. Use the targets below as a checklist: can you do each one without notes?

  • 6.1 I can classify quadrilaterals with an inclusive family tree.
  • 6.2 I can prove opposite sides and angles of a parallelogram are equal.
  • 6.3 I can prove the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
  • 6.4 I can use sufficient conditions to prove a parallelogram.
  • 6.5 I can prove properties of special parallelograms.
  • 6.6 I can prove properties of isosceles trapezoids and kites.
  • 6.7 I can prove the triangle midsegment is parallel to the third side and half as long.
  • 6.8 I can prove a quadrilateral is a parallelogram on the coordinate plane using slopes and midpoints.
  • 6.9 I can develop and use formulas for interior angle sums and the exterior angle sum of a convex polygon.
  • 6.10 I can find angle measures of regular polygons and star polygons.

slides.title: Practice: 6.1
slides.html: Is every square a rectangle? Is every rectangle a square?
slides.reveal: Every square is a rectangle (four right angles). Not every rectangle is a square; its sides need not all be equal.

slides.title: Practice: 6.4
slides.html: Two pencils of different lengths cross at their midpoints. What shape do the four ends make?
slides.reveal: A parallelogram, because the diagonals bisect each other.

slides.title: Common traps
slides.html:
Watch out for these common mistakes:

  • a square is not a rectangle
  • every property of a parallelogram is also a test for one
  • trapezoid definitions (exclusive vs. inclusive) are the same
  • exterior angle sum depends on number of sides
